newsitem.title: UK: Hollick making his mark at United News.
newsitem.headline: Hollick making his mark at United News.

text.p: United News & Media Plc's agreed bid for Blenheim Plc on Tuesday marked the latest success for United News chief Clive Hollick, a left-leaning lord who built his career with ambitious acquisitions.

Hollick, who was made a peer in 1991 at the request of former Labour leader Neil Kinnock, merged his MAI television and financial services conglomerate with United News earlier this year in a deal that surprised the market.

The marriage spawned the so-called odd couple of Hollick, the son of a humble French polisher, and United News chairman Lord Stevens, whose Daily Express and Daily Star tabloids reflect Stevens' strong support for the ruling Conservatives.
Hollick, 51, a trim, bearded man with angular features, is seen by analysts as an astute business manager who keeps a tight rein on costs.
United News' offering for Blenheim, which valued the exhibitions group at 592.5 million pounds ($937.9 million) bore the hallmark of Hollick's aggressive management style, analysts said.
Hollick beat off competition from Dutch publisher VNU, which said Tuesday it would not launch a counter-bid for Blenheim and would likely sell the 15 percent stake it bought in the company last week.
Brought up in the southern city of Southampton where he went to a local state school, Hollick studied politics, psychology and sociology at Nottingham University in the Midlands.
He got his first big business break in 1974, when aristocratic investment bank Hambros put the then 29-year-old in charge of the failed commercial bank Vavasseur.
Instead of guiding it into peaceful liquidation, Hollick transformed it into the major money-broker later known as MAI.
In 1991 MAI thrust itself into broadcasting with a successful 36 million pound bid to run the TV franchise in England's affluent south and south-east regions.
That presence was cemented in 1994 with the 292 million pound takover of east England franchise-holder Anglia TV.
Hollick's supporters have been reported as saying he has no ambitions to be a front-stage player on the political scene.

Challenged on how he reconciles his millionaire status with the doctrine of socialism, he has been quoted as replying: "A passion for social justice and equal opportunities is entirely consistent with a desire to build a successful business." ($1=.6317 Pound)
